title: Hybrid Quantum-Classical Models and Optimization Techniques for Financial Fraud Detection
journal_or_venue: Proceedings of the 6th International Conference on IoT Based Control Networks and Intelligent Systems (ICICNIS-2025) (IEEE)
abstract_summary: The paper proposes a hybrid quantum–classical fraud detection pipeline that integrates Quantum Support Vector Machine (QSVM), Variational Quantum Classifier (VQC), classical SVM and KNN, and a QUBO-based ensemble fusion to improve detection on highly imbalanced financial transaction data. Evaluated on the original European credit card fraud dataset using Qiskit Aer simulators, the approach reports higher recall, reduced false negatives, and improved precision and F1 when using the QUBO-driven ensemble, and the authors discuss future hardware validation and scalability studies.
methodology_description: The study implements an end-to-end hybrid quantum–classical fraud detection pipeline evaluated on the original (highly imbalanced) European credit card fraud dataset. Preprocessing included Min–Max normalization for Time and Amount, optional imputation (not required for this dataset), SMOTE oversampling and class-weighted losses to mitigate class imbalance, and stratified splitting into train/validation/test (70%/15%/15%) with 5-fold cross-validation for robustness. Feature engineering combined classical PCA (preserving original anonymized V1–V28 PCA features) and a Quantum Feature Selection (QFS) stage; PCA-reduced components (20 for QSVM experiments) served as inputs to quantum models. Two quantum learners were trained in simulation: a QSVM using a ZZFeatureMap (2 layers) and a fidelity-based quantum kernel plugged into a classical SVM dual formulation (C=1.0) on a Qiskit Aer statevector simulator, and a Variational Quantum Classifier (VQC) with angle encoding, a ZZFeatureMap encoder, a RealAmplitudes ansatz (2 layers, full entanglement), measurement via Pauli-Z expectation, and optimization with the derivative-free COBYLA optimizer (max iterations = 300). Classical learners (SVM, KNN) were trained in parallel as baselines. Predictions from QSVM, VQC, SVM and KNN were fused using a QUBO-based ensemble selection: each base learner had a binary selection variable, the QUBO matrix incorporated classifier error and inter-classifier correlation (Qii = α Err + λ; Qij = β Corr), and simulated annealing solved the QUBO (α=1.0, β=0.5, λ=0.1). Final ensemble decisions used majority voting over the selected models. Performance was reported using accuracy, precision, recall, F1, ROC-AUC and PR-AUC; comparisons were made between individual quantum models and the QUBO-optimized hybrid ensemble.
experimental_setup: Simulated quantum experiments using Qiskit Aer statevector backend for QSVM and VQC; QUBO ensemble solved via simulated annealing (classical solver). Classical models (SVM, KNN) trained on the same PCA-reduced and balanced (SMOTE / class-weighted) data. Train/validation/test split = 70/15/15 stratified; 5-fold cross-validation used for classical baselines.
dataset_used: European credit card transactions dataset (Kaggle, September 2013) with 284,807 transactions, 492 fraudulent (class imbalance ≈ 0.173%), 30 features (28 anonymized PCA components V1–V28 plus Time and Amount), target variable Class (0/1).

reproducibility_notes: The dataset used is a public Kaggle dataset (European credit card fraud 2013). The paper specifies model architectures, feature engineering steps, optimizer settings, PCA component count, QUBO formulation and hyperparameters. However, no code repository, configuration files, exact random seeds, nor explicit qubit counts and measurement shot numbers are provided in the text, and experiments were performed on a simulator rather than hardware. Reproducing exact numeric results is feasible in principle given the provided hyperparameters and the public dataset, but would require reimplementation details (encoding mapping, QFS implementation, training seeds and specific simulated annealing configuration) which are not included.
key_findings: [supported] The paper implements and evaluates a hybrid quantum–classical fraud detection pipeline combining QSVM, VQC, classical SVM and KNN, trained on the original (highly imbalanced) European credit card fraud dataset.
[supported] Experiments were run on Qiskit Aer statevector simulators (no quantum hardware experiments reported).
[supported] The proposed QUBO-based ensemble fusion improved aggregate classification metrics relative to the individual quantum classifiers reported in the study.
[supported] QSVM (with a fidelity-based quantum kernel on PCA-reduced features) produced strong recall but modest precision in the experiments.
[supported] VQC (RealAmplitudes ansatz, COBYLA optimizer) favored recall over precision in the reported experiments.

[supported] The dataset and preprocessing choices: original dataset of 284,807 transactions (492 frauds), PCA for dimensionality reduction, SMOTE and class-weighting used to address imbalance, and stratified splits with 5-fold CV for robustness.

[speculative] The paper claims a novel QUBO-based ensemble selection mechanism for fraud detection and states ("to the best of our knowledge") that this is the first application of QUBO-driven fusion to fraud detection.

[speculative] The authors claim that combining quantum feature selection (QFS) with PCA preserves nonlinear interactions and benefits model performance; this is proposed as a novel feature-engineering strategy.

[speculative] The paper asserts that hybrid quantum–classical techniques can improve on classical systems by increasing recall, reducing false negatives, and speeding detection of new fraud types—some parts of this are suggested by simulator results but other aspects (notably detection speed and hardware advantage) are not demonstrated.

[speculative] The work claims empirical validation beyond conceptual studies; while it does report simulator-based experiments on the original dataset, deployment, hardware validation, and real-time production operation remain future work.
results_summary: The authors build a hybrid quantum–classical fraud-detection pipeline (QSVM, VQC, classical SVM/KNN) with PCA + quantum feature selection preprocessing and a QUBO-based ensemble selector. Experiments run on a statevector simulator using the original, highly imbalanced European credit card dataset show that the QUBO-selected ensemble outperforms the individual quantum models in the reported metrics (notably higher precision, F1, ROC-AUC and PR-AUC). The study demonstrates simulator-based improvements in detection metrics but does not report hardware experiments or direct comparisons to strong classical baselines (e.g., tuned Random Forests, XGBoost) in the paper, and claims about runtime speedups and real-world deployment remain unproven.
performance_claims: [supported] QUBO hybrid ensemble: Accuracy 0.999, Precision 0.42, Recall 0.76, F1 Score 0.54, ROC-AUC 0.94, PR-AUC 0.47 (reported from simulator experiments).
[supported] QSVM (fidelity-based kernel on 20 PCA components): Accuracy 0.998, Precision 0.25, Recall 0.72, F1 Score 0.37, ROC-AUC 0.91, PR-AUC 0.32 (reported from simulator experiments).
[supported] VQC (RealAmplitudes ansatz, COBYLA): Accuracy 0.997, Precision 0.18, Recall 0.80, F1 Score 0.29, ROC-AUC 0.90, PR-AUC 0.28 (reported from simulator experiments).
[supported] Dataset statistics: total transactions 284,807; fraudulent 492; legitimate 284,315; fraud ratio ≈ 0.173% (~1:577) (reported).
quantum_advantage_detail: The paper reports improved classification metrics for a QUBO-selected hybrid ensemble in statevector simulator experiments, but does not demonstrate an experimental quantum advantage on physical quantum hardware nor isolate performance gains attributable solely to quantum processing (some gains plausibly arise from classical ensemble optimization and preprocessing). Therefore claims of quantum advantage are speculative and not empirically established in this work.
limitations: Use of a simulated quantum backend rather than execution on real quantum hardware (authors acknowledge results rely on simulation).
Scalability constraints as qubit count increases (noted by authors as a complexity/limitation for QSVM).
Variational Quantum Classifier limitations: optimizer convergence issues and circuit depth constraints (authors state VQC is limited by optimizer convergence and circuit depth).
QUBO ensemble solved using classical simulated annealing in experiments (the work does not evaluate performance using actual quantum annealers).
Evaluation performed on a single publicly available dataset (European credit card fraud) — limits demonstrated diversity and cross-domain generalizability. [inferred]
Extreme class imbalance of the dataset (0.173% fraud) makes evaluation and reported metrics sensitive and may limit generalization to other fraud contexts (authors note challenges from imbalance).
Dependence on PCA for dimensionality reduction may remove discriminative information or obscure features useful for quantum encodings. [inferred]
Use of SMOTE and other synthetic oversampling to mitigate imbalance may introduce artifacts and does not guarantee realistic minority-class modelling. [inferred]

Limited discussion and evaluation of real-time deployment constraints (latency, throughput) and whether the hybrid pipeline meets operational requirements (authors note need for real-time monitoring but do not fully validate it). [inferred]

Interpretability and explainability of hybrid quantum–classical decisions are not addressed in depth (paper highlights interpretability issues of classical models but does not present explainability solutions for the hybrid system). [inferred]
Unclear sensitivity to hyperparameter choices (e.g., QUBO weights α, β, λ; SVM C; VQC optimizer settings) and lack of ablation or sensitivity analysis. [inferred]
Potential effects of quantum/noise on model robustness are not evaluated (simulation omits hardware noise models). [inferred]

Comparative baseline coverage is narrow — limited comparison with stronger classical baselines (e.g., deep learning, graph-based semi-supervised models, advanced ensembles) or industry production systems. [inferred]

Operational concerns such as model drift detection, retraining frequency, monitoring costs and integration with production fraud pipelines are discussed at high level but not quantitatively evaluated. (authors note practical deployment considerations are often missing in literature).
